opus-5.5.text:
I think what stood out most was how small and cross-functional it was from the very beginning. It wasn't a traditional setup where research hands something off to product and then design gets brought in at the end. We had research, engineering, design, and product people sitting together from day one, iterating on the same thing at the same time.

That mattered because Canvas was as much a model behavior problem as an interface problem. Questions like when the model should open a canvas, how it should make targeted edits instead of rewriting everything, and how it should leave comments the way a collaborator would were all deeply tied to how the experience felt. So the designers were thinking about model behavior, and the researchers were thinking about the user experience. Those boundaries got really blurry, in a good way.

The other distinctive thing was how much we leaned on rapid prototyping and on synthetic data to teach the model these new behaviors. Instead of waiting for large amounts of human data, we could define the behavior we wanted, generate training data for it, train, look at the outputs, and adjust quickly. That tight loop between "here's the product intuition" and "here's the model actually doing it" let a fairly small group move fast.

And honestly, people just cared a lot. There was a shared belief that the chat interface alone wasn't the end state for working with these models, and that we needed something that felt more like collaborating with a partner on writing or code. That conviction kept everyone pulling in the same direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies the team’s small, cross-functional setup from day one as distinctive, but does not say the team formed spontaneously.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most distinctive thing was that Canvas was never really a product-management-driven project. It started as a small group of us who were actually using ChatGPT every day for writing and coding and feeling the friction ourselves. The chat interface is great for conversation, but the moment you're iterating on something longer, a document, a piece of code, you're constantly scrolling back, copying things out, losing the thread. So the motivation was very personal before it was strategic.

The second thing is that it was genuinely a research-and-product team from day one, not research handing something off to product. We had people doing post-training sitting next to designers and engineers. That mattered because Canvas isn't just a UI, the model has to know when to open a canvas, when to make a targeted edit versus rewrite everything, how to leave comments instead of silently changing your work. Those are model behaviors, and you can't design them in Figma. You have to train for them, evaluate them, and then watch real people use them and go back and fix the model. We did that loop constantly, sometimes in the same week.

And honestly, the team was small. That's underrated. When a handful of people own the whole stack, from the data and the evals to the pixels, you don't spend your time negotiating interfaces between teams. You spend it trying things. A lot of what ended up shipping came from someone building a rough prototype over a weekend, using it themselves, and realizing the interaction felt right before anyone could write a spec for it.

So I'd say: a felt need rather than a roadmap item, research and product truly intertwined, and a team small enough to move on intuition and then verify it.

r001.rationale: The response says Canvas began with a small group who felt the need while using ChatGPT, but it does not clearly identify the team’s spontaneous formation as its most distinctive feature.

astra-6.text: I think the most distinctive thing was how closely research and product came together. With Canvas, the model’s behavior and the interface really depend on each other: when should the model edit directly, when should it leave a comment, and when should it just respond in chat? Those are both research questions and design questions. So it was a very collaborative process, where shaping the experience also meant shaping what we wanted the model to learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes close collaboration between research and product, but does not say the team formed spontaneously.

sol-6.1.text: What stood out to me was how closely research, design, and engineering worked together from the beginning. We weren’t just building a model and then figuring out what interface to put around it. We were exploring the interaction and the model behavior together: What should happen when you highlight a paragraph? When should the model rewrite something versus leave a comment? Those product questions became research questions, and what we learned from the model shaped the product. That was a really collaborative way to build.

r001.rationale: The response describes close collaboration among research, design, and engineering from the beginning, but does not say the team formed spontaneously.
